implementation_notes: Spring Integration is the dominant Java realization: annotate a method of a managed object with @ServiceActivator(inputChannel = ...) and the framework extracts the message payload into the method argument, invokes it on the consuming thread and sends a non-null return value to the configured output channel or to the request's replyChannel header, while a thrown exception becomes an ErrorMessage on the errorChannel. The endpoint object of the classic structure is replaced by a MessageHandler created from the bean method. Prefer it whenever the flow also needs routing, polling, transactions or SpEL-based dispatch.
pitfalls: A null return sends no reply, and with requires-reply enabled it raises ReplyRequiredException; an accidental null therefore looks like a deliberate one-way endpoint.
The endpoint runs on the consuming or poller thread by default, so a long blocking service call stalls the channel's dispatcher unless async handling or a poller executor is configured.
A POJO signature hides the envelope: headers the service needs (correlation id, return address) must be pulled in explicitly with @Header, otherwise the reply cannot be correlated.

variants.name: Virtual-thread dispatcher: one virtual thread per message (Java 21)
variants.implementation_notes: On Java 21 the endpoint can submit every message to its own virtual thread, so a service written in plain blocking style (JDBC, synchronous HTTP) scales with message rate without a bounded pool; the activator only builds the argument, submits the task and maps result or exception back to the reply and error channels. Choose it when blocking service code would otherwise exhaust a platform-thread pool; keep the annotation form when the flow needs channels, pollers and transactions.
pitfalls: Virtual threads make blocking cheap but bound nothing: unbounded submission still exhausts memory and downstream connections, so the channel needs backpressure or a semaphore.
The same service instance is now entered concurrently, whereas a single-threaded poller hid the sharing; thread-safety becomes the service's problem.
The reply is sent from the task rather than the dispatcher, so the acknowledgement is no longer part of the dispatcher's transaction and commit order must be handled explicitly.
